{"assessment_summary":"This manuscript makes an ambitious and consequential claim—global warming damages world GDP far more than prior panel estimates—by shifting identification from local (country) temperature variation to time-series variation in global mean temperature. The empirical core is a set of time-series and panel local-projection estimates of world/country GDP responses to “global temperature shocks,” defined as multi-step forecast errors from a Hamilton (2018) detrending/innovation procedure. The headline response is large (≈12% peak GDP loss per +1°C global shock at ~6 years) and persistent, and the paper then maps these reduced-form responses into a structural productivity damage kernel in a neoclassical growth model to compute large welfare losses and an SCC above $1,000/tCO2.

The most important technical concern is identification in a short global time series. Even with many robustness checks, the design fundamentally relies on the assumption that innovations to global temperature (after removing predictable components and adding macro controls) are as-good-as-random with respect to other global shocks that affect GDP at multi-year horizons. This is much harder to guarantee than in subnational/country panel designs. The time-series sample for the headline estimate is ~60 annual observations (1960–2019). With local projections out to 10 years, inference and finite-sample robustness are delicate: overlapping dependent variables (cumulative growth), persistent regressors (their shock has autocorrelation by construction), and multiple controls/dummies consume degrees of freedom. The authors use lag augmentation and various controls; however, small-sample distortions, sensitivity of long-horizon LPs, and implicit researcher degrees of freedom (horizon choice, lags, controls, recession dummies, filtering choices) remain potential threats. The paper provides many alternative specifications and finds similar shapes, which is reassuring, but the “global shock” setting remains more vulnerable to unobserved common factors than local-weather panel work.

A second concern is conceptual: whether “natural variability” shocks to global mean temperature are externally valid for damages from anthropogenic warming. The paper argues that global mean temperature is the relevant state variable and that global shocks better predict extremes than idiosyncratic local shocks; still, natural variability episodes (ENSO, volcanic forcing, solar) differ from sustained radiative forcing in spatial pattern, seasonality, ocean/land distribution, and the joint behavior of other climate variables. Even if the authors show robustness to controlling for ENSO and volcano years, the remaining variation is still a mix of mechanisms. The mapping from these historical deviations to a smooth +2°C path by 2100 assumes (i) local-linear damages in temperature over a range much larger than realized annual global shocks (~0.3°C max), and (ii) stability of the joint relationship between global temperature and damaging extremes under different forcing regimes. The manuscript discusses nonlinearity briefly and finds little evidence within-sample, but the data are not informative about tails and tipping behavior; equally, they are not very informative about large-scale adaptation under slow, anticipated warming.

Third, the interpretation of the 12% “per 1°C shock” is subtle because their shock is persistent in temperature levels. The GDP impulse response partly reflects accumulated exposure to elevated temperatures following the shock, not just the contemporaneous 1°C increase. They provide a decomposition that yields a smaller peak effect (~5%) for a purely transitory temperature increase. For welfare/SCC, the crucial object is the damage kernel (the mapping from a temperature path to productivity), and here the identification hinges on correctly estimating both (a) the temperature persistence response and (b) the GDP response. Any bias in persistence (from filtering choices) can mechanically amplify the inferred long-run damages.

Fourth, the “extreme events” mechanism is suggestive but not fully pinned down causally. The paper shows global temperature shocks predict increases in several reanalysis-based extreme indices, whereas local shocks do not, and a bottom-up aggregation explains ~two-thirds of the GDP response. However, measurement choices (percentile thresholds, baseline 1950–1980, smoothing of wind/precipitation, reanalysis quality in early decades, cross-country aggregation) and potential simultaneous global shocks affecting both extremes reporting/measurement and economic activity could influence these results. The aggregation exercise mixes dynamic responses and requires assumptions about persistence and separability across channels; it is informative, but not a definitive mediation analysis.

Fifth, the structural translation to welfare and SCC, while transparent, is model-dependent. The neoclassical growth model is intentionally simple (representative agent, exogenous labor, no climate adaptation investment, no endogenous mitigation, no sectoral/region heterogeneity). The estimated “damage function” is effectively a reduced-form productivity kernel that absorbs all channels; that is consistent with a top-down approach, but it also means the SCC is sensitive to (i) assuming damages operate only through TFP (not depreciation, mortality, amenities, risk, inequality), (ii) the functional-form restriction used to extrapolate beyond the 10-year empirical horizon, (iii) the assumption of persistent level effects rather than growth effects, and (iv) the assumed future temperature path and discounting. The authors do a fair amount of sensitivity analysis for discounting and warming levels, but uncertainty propagation remains partial: e.g., uncertainty in climate sensitivity/impulse response, in the representativeness of historical variability, and in long-horizon extrapolation of the damage kernel is not fully integrated.

Finally, replicability and transparency look decent in terms of data provenance (public datasets, detailed appendices, many robustness figures), but the paper does not clearly state code/data release, versioning, and exact pipelines for constructing shocks and extreme indices; given the complexity (multiple datasets, weighting schemes, filters, and smoothing), full computational reproducibility would depend on sharing code and intermediate artifacts.

Overall, this is a high-quality, carefully executed contribution with extensive robustness work and a clear argument for why global temperature may capture damages that local-temperature panel designs difference out. The key uncertainty is whether the time-series identification and external validity are strong enough to support the magnitude of the headline effect and the resulting SCC; even moderate attenuation from residual confounding or non-representativeness could materially change welfare numbers. The paper’s strengths—novel perspective, comprehensive datasets, and transparent mapping to welfare—are substantial, but readers should treat the quantitative magnitudes as more uncertain than the within-paper confidence intervals imply, because several deep uncertainties are not (and arguably cannot be) fully identified from the historical time series used here.","key_issues":["1) Time-series identification risk: global temperature innovations may still correlate with unobserved global shocks (policy, finance, technology, geopolitics) that affect GDP at multi-year horizons, and the small annual sample (≈60) makes this hard to rule out conclusively.","2) External validity: natural variability shocks (ENSO/volcano/other internal variability) may not be representative of damages from sustained anthropogenic warming, due to different spatial/seasonal patterns and joint dynamics of climate variables.","3) Magnitude interpretation: the 12% “per 1°C shock” effect partly reflects the post-shock persistence of temperature; the welfare mapping depends critically on how persistence is estimated and translated into a damage kernel.","4) Limited information about nonlinearities and tails: the historical global shocks are small; extrapolating linearly to multi-degree warming and to potential tipping points/adaptation regimes is weakly identified.","5) Long-horizon LP and finite-sample inference: overlapping cumulative-growth outcomes, persistent regressors, multiple controls/dummies, and 10-year horizons can generate biased standard errors and sensitivity to specification choices despite robustness checks.","6) Temperature-shock construction: the Hamilton (2018) multi-step forecast-error approach (choice of h and p) is defensible but not uniquely grounded; shock definitions can embed assumptions about persistence that influence implied damages.","7) Mediation via extreme events is suggestive but not causal: extreme indices rely on reanalysis and threshold/smoothing choices; the bottom-up aggregation assumes separability and correct dynamic persistence and may omit other correlated channels.","8) Panel-country evidence still lacks time fixed effects for global shocks; while global controls and alternative designs are explored, any residual common-factor confounding remains a concern.","9) Structural welfare/SCC translation is model-dependent: representative-agent neoclassical model with damages only through TFP omits adaptation, sectoral/region heterogeneity, risk/uncertainty, and endogenous mitigation; the functional-form restriction for the damage kernel extrapolates beyond observed horizons.","10) Uncertainty propagation: reported confidence intervals mainly reflect reduced-form estimation uncertainty; deeper uncertainties (climate impulse response, external validity, long-horizon extrapolation, measurement error in extremes) are not fully integrated.","11) Replicability: while data sources are public and appendices are detailed, full computational reproducibility likely requires releasing code and exact data-processing pipelines (shocks, weighting, extreme event construction, smoothing choices, and versioning)."],"metrics":{"overall":{"midpoint":86,"lower_bound":76,"upper_bound":92},"claims_evidence":{"midpoint":82,"lower_bound":70,"upper_bound":90},"methods":{"midpoint":79,"lower_bound":66,"upper_bound":88},"advancing_knowledge":{"midpoint":91,"lower_bound":83,"upper_bound":96},"logic_communication":{"midpoint":87,"lower_bound":78,"upper_bound":93},"open_science":{"midpoint":58,"lower_bound":40,"upper_bound":75},"global_relevance":{"midpoint":96,"lower_bound":90,"upper_bound":99},"tier_should":{"score":4.4,"ci_lower":3.7,"ci_upper":4.9},"tier_will":{"score":4.1,"ci_lower":3.2,"ci_upper":4.8}}}
